7 residuals: largest / smallest SD of the eight cells 1.17 reported – 
plot_residuals(h3_model)

The model converges, two other optimizers give the same fixed effects, every variance lies above zero, and the residuals and the person intercepts stay within the bounds of normality; the residuals spread about evenly over condition and wave (the largest SD of a cell is 1.17 times the smallest).

Next → Step 2, the random structure: Is the municipality a level of its own?

Step 2 · The random structure both groups

Is the municipality a level of its own? The null model with persons nested in municipalities, against persons alone:

h3_null_person <- lmer(H3_Wellbeing ~ 1 + (1 | id),
                       data = df)
h3_null_nested <- lmer(H3_Wellbeing ~ 1 + (1 | Municipality/id),
                       data = df)

AIC(h3_null_person, h3_null_nested) |>
  mutate(AIC = round(AIC, 1))
df AIC
h3_null_person 3 2897.4
h3_null_nested 4 2892.2

How is the variance shared? In the null model with both levels:

h3_shares <- as_tibble(VarCorr(h3_null_nested)) |>
  transmute(level = grp, variance = vcov, share = vcov / sum(vcov))

h3_shares |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))
level variance share
id:Municipality 0.735 0.642
Municipality 0.043 0.038
Residual 0.366 0.320

And the trainers? The model of step 1 with the trainers as a further level, and its variances:

h3_trainer <- lmer(H3_Wellbeing ~ Occasion * condition +
                     (1 | trainedBy/Municipality/id),
                   data = df,
                   control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))

AIC(h3_model, h3_trainer) |>
  mutate(AIC = round(AIC, 1))
df AIC
h3_model 11 2892.8
h3_trainer 12 2894.8 
h3_trainer_shares <- as_tibble(VarCorr(h3_trainer)) |>
  transmute(level = grp, variance = vcov, share = vcov / sum(vcov))

h3_trainer_shares |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))
level variance share
id:Municipality:trainedBy 0.738 0.657
Municipality:trainedBy 0.030 0.026
trainedBy 0.002 0.002
Residual 0.353 0.314

AIC prefers persons nested in municipalities to persons alone, by 5.2 points. Of the variance, 3.8 % lies between the municipalities, 64.2 % between the persons of a municipality and 32.0 % between the questionnaires of a person. The trainer level takes up 0.2 % of the variance but does not lower the AIC (it rises by 2.0 points). The model of step 1 stays.

Next → Step 3, the interactions: Does the experimental group change more?

The effects · Steps 3 to 5

Step 3 · The interactions both groups

Does the experimental group change more? The three interaction terms, with and without the trainer level:

h3_trainer_fixed <- tidy(h3_trainer, effects = "fixed") |>
  select(term, b_trainer = estimate, p_trainer = p.value)

h3_interactions <- h3_fixed |>
  filter(str_detect(term, ":")) |>
  left_join(h3_trainer_fixed, by = "term")

h3_interactions |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))
term b se df p b_trainer p_trainer
OccasionT1:conditionExperimental 0.167 0.097 715.264 0.084 0.168 0.084
OccasionT2:conditionExperimental 0.180 0.107 763.186 0.095 0.180 0.095
OccasionT3:conditionExperimental 0.062 0.118 743.685 0.597 0.063 0.596

What does the model imply? The means of both groups at each wave; shaded the two training windows:

plot_means(h3_model)

By T1 the experimental group has not gained significantly more than the control group (b = 0.17, p = .084), nor by T2 (b = 0.18, p = .095). At T3, after the control group’s training, the groups do not differ significantly either (b = 0.06, p = .597). With the trainer level, the three terms stay the same to three decimals and keep their verdicts.

Next → Step 4, one-sided tests: Does it hold one-sided?

Step 4 · One-sided tests both groups

Does it hold one-sided? The effects at T1 and T2, where the hypotheses expect a positive sign:

h3_one_sided <- h3_interactions |>
  filter(term != "OccasionT3:conditionExperimental") |>
  transmute(term, b, p, p_one_sided = pt(b / se, df, lower.tail = FALSE))

h3_one_sided |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))
term b p p_one_sided
OccasionT1:conditionExperimental 0.167 0.084 0.042
OccasionT2:conditionExperimental 0.180 0.095 0.047

One-sided, both effects become significant (p = .042 at T1, p = .047 at T2).

Next → Step 5, the replication: Does the control group gain when it trains?

Step 5 · The replication both groups

Does the control group gain when it trains? The period-specific model, on the September and December waves:

h3_period <- lmer(H3_Wellbeing ~ condition * Time_T3 +
                    (1 | Municipality/id),
                  data = df_T23)

h3_period_terms <- tidy(h3_period, effects = "fixed") |>
  filter(str_detect(term, ":")) |>
  transmute(term, b = estimate, se = std.error, df, p = p.value,
            singular = isSingular(h3_period))

h3_period_terms |>
  mutate(p_one_sided = pt(-b / se, df, lower.tail = FALSE),
         across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))
term b se df p singular p_one_sided
conditionExperimental:Time_T3 -0.209 0.114 206.425 0.068 FALSE 0.034

And over all four waves? The piecewise model, with one time indicator for each training:

h3_piecewise <- lmer(H3_Wellbeing ~ condition *
                       (Time_Exp_Training + Time_Control_Training) +
                       (1 | Municipality/id),
                     data = df)

h3_piecewise_terms <- tidy(h3_piecewise, effects = "fixed") |>
  filter(str_detect(term, ":")) |>
  transmute(term, b = estimate, se = std.error, df, p = p.value)

h3_piecewise_terms |>
  mutate(expected    = if_else(str_detect(term, "Time_Exp"), 1, -1),
         p_one_sided = pt(expected * b / se, df, lower.tail = FALSE),
         across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))
term b se df p expected p_one_sided
conditionExperimental:Time_Exp_Training 0.168 0.085 738.491 0.049 1 0.025
conditionExperimental:Time_Control_Training -0.104 0.108 720.697 0.334 -1 0.167

Between September and December, while the control group trains, it does not gain significantly more than the experimental group (b = -0.21, p = .068). In the piecewise model the experimental group gains more while it trains (b = 0.17, p = .049), and the control group’s window shows no significant effect (b = -0.10, p = .334).

What does a single indicator of being trained show? D is 1 once a person’s own group has trained (Chapter 2):

h3_D <- lmer(H3_Wellbeing ~ D + (1 | Municipality/id),
             data = df)

tidy(h3_D, effects = "fixed") |>
  filter(term == "D") |>
  select(term, b = estimate, se = std.error, df, p = p.value) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))
term b se df p
D 0.23 0.042 757.922 0

Being trained goes with a score higher by 0.23 points (p < .001). Without time effects, D also takes up any general improvement over the year, so this is an upper bound of the training effect.

Next → Step 6, random slopes: Does the change vary within each condition?

Robustness · Steps 6 and 7

Step 6 · Random slopes both groups

Does the change vary within each condition? The eight tests of the script (10.2), four in each condition:

h3_slopes_within <- slopes_within |>
  filter(outcome == "H3_Wellbeing") |>
  select(-outcome)

h3_slopes_within |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))
condition test chisq df p
Experimental slopes, municipalities 0.428 5 0.995
Experimental slope T0 vs. later, persons 0.276 2 0.871
Experimental slope T3 vs. earlier, persons 0.236 2 0.889
Experimental municipality x pre/post 6.351 9 0.704
Control slopes, municipalities 4.395 5 0.494
Control slope T0 vs. later, persons 7.556 2 0.023
Control slope T3 vs. earlier, persons 6.834 2 0.033
Control municipality x pre/post 4.273 9 0.893

Two of the eight tests are significant, both in the control group: the slope of T0 against later across persons and the slope of T3 against earlier across persons. In neither condition do the municipalities gain differently from their own training.

And across trainers and municipalities? Random slopes of both time contrasts at the trainer and municipality levels, against random intercepts, on maximum-likelihood fits:

h3_intercepts <- lmer(H3_Wellbeing ~ TF_helmert + TS_helmert +
                        (1 | trainedBy/Municipality) + (1 | id),
                      data = df, REML = FALSE)
h3_slopes <- lmer(H3_Wellbeing ~ TF_helmert + TS_helmert +
                    (TF_helmert + TS_helmert | trainedBy/Municipality) +
                    (1 | id),
                  data = df, REML = FALSE)

h3_slope_test <- anova(h3_intercepts, h3_slopes)

h3_slope_test |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))
npar AIC BIC logLik -2*log(L) Chisq Df Pr(>Chisq)
h3_intercepts 7 2863.370 2898.642 -1424.685 2849.370 NA NA NA
h3_slopes 17 2878.636 2964.295 -1422.318 2844.636 4.735 10 0.908

Across trainers and municipalities, the slopes of both contrasts do not improve the model significantly (χ²(10) = 4.7, p = .908).

Next → Step 7, equivalence: Which random structure is the richest?

Step 7 · Equivalence both groups

Which random structure is the richest? The model of step 1 under the three structures, fitted with bobyqa, and the smallest variance of each:

h3_structures <- list(
  `(1 | trainedBy/Municipality/id)` = h3_trainer,
  `(1 | Municipality/id)` =
    lmer(H3_Wellbeing ~ Occasion * condition +
           (1 | Municipality/id),
         data = df, control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")),
  `(1 | id)` =
    lmer(H3_Wellbeing ~ Occasion * condition +
           (1 | id),
         data = df, control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")))

h3_variances <- h3_structures |>
  map(\(fit) as_tibble(VarCorr(fit))) |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "structure") |>
  summarise(smallest = min(vcov), .by = structure) |>
  mutate(above_zero = smallest >= 1e-8)

h3_variances |>
  mutate(smallest = sprintf("%.1e", smallest))
structure smallest above_zero
(1 | trainedBy/Municipality/id) 2.1e-03 TRUE
(1 | Municipality/id) 3.2e-02 TRUE
(1 | id) 3.5e-01 TRUE 
# the first structure whose variances all lie above zero
h3_richest <- h3_variances$structure[h3_variances$above_zero][1]

Do the groups really not differ? The two claims of absence, at baseline and after both trainings, with the preregistered and with the richest structure:

h3_sd_T0 <- sd(df$H3_Wellbeing[df$Occasion == "T0"], na.rm = TRUE)

h3_tost <- bind_rows(
  preregistered = tidy(h3_model, effects = "fixed"),
  richest       = tidy(h3_structures[[h3_richest]], effects = "fixed"),
  .id = "model") |>
  filter(term %in% c("conditionExperimental",
                     "OccasionT3:conditionExperimental")) |>
  transmute(model,
            claim   = if_else(term == "conditionExperimental", "baseline",
                              "after_both"),
            term,
            delta_d = estimate / h3_sd_T0,
            se_d    = std.error / h3_sd_T0,
            ci_low  = delta_d - qt(.95, df) * se_d,
            ci_high = delta_d + qt(.95, df) * se_d,
            p_tost  = pmax(pt((delta_d + sesoi) / se_d, df,
                              lower.tail = FALSE),
                           pt((delta_d - sesoi) / se_d, df)),
            p_two_sided = p.value,
            verdict = verdict_of(p_tost, p_two_sided))

h3_tost |>
  select(model, claim, delta_d, ci_low, ci_high, p_tost, p_two_sided,
         verdict) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))
model claim delta_d ci_low ci_high p_tost p_two_sided verdict
preregistered baseline -0.206 -0.414 0.002 0.519 0.103 inconclusive
preregistered after_both 0.057 -0.121 0.236 0.095 0.597 inconclusive
richest baseline -0.206 -0.420 0.008 0.519 0.112 inconclusive
richest after_both 0.058 -0.121 0.236 0.095 0.596 inconclusive

Neither claim of absence can be shown. Both tests are inconclusive, as their intervals reach beyond ±0.20: at baseline Δd = -0.21, 90 % CI [-0.41, 0.00], after both trainings Δd = 0.06, 90 % CI [-0.12, 0.24]. The richest structure with all variances above zero keeps the trainer level, persons in municipalities in trainers; it gives the same verdicts, and Δd stays the same to three decimals.

Next → Step 8, what follows: Where does the result go?

What follows · Step 8

Step 8 · What follows

Where does the result go? Well-being reaches significance at T1 and T2 only one-sided, and in the experimental group’s window of the piecewise model; the control group does not gain significantly more when it trains. Its interaction at T1 is the preregistered test of Hypothesis 3: 10.7 corrects it within the three composites, Chapter 14 repeats the model in every sample set, and Chapter 20 sets it beside the other estimates of the training effect.

10.7 Many outcomes at once

Which tests are corrected? Each hypothesis is tested on many outcomes at once. The directional tests of the 26 sections come together in three tables: the interactions (step 3), the period-specific terms and the piecewise terms (step 5):

interactions <- from_sections("interactions") |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "outcome") |>
  transmute(outcome, term, b, se, df, p,
            wave = str_extract(term, "T[1-3]"))

period_specific <- from_sections("period_terms") |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "outcome") |>
  select(outcome, singular, term, b, se, df, p)

piecewise <- from_sections("piecewise_terms") |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "outcome") |>
  mutate(training = if_else(str_detect(term, "Time_Exp"), "experimental",
                            "control"))

With which sign? The experimental group should gain more by T1 and keep its advantage at T2 (positive interactions); the control group should gain more while it trains (negative terms in the period-specific model and in the second term of the piecewise model), while the first piecewise term should be positive. The one-sided p as in step 4:

# the directional tests of steps 3 and 5, with the sign they expect
directional <- bind_rows(
  interactions |>
    filter(wave %in% c("T1", "T2")) |>
    transmute(test = str_c("preregistered, ", wave), outcome, b, se, df, p,
              expected = 1),
  period_specific |>
    transmute(test = "period-specific, T3", outcome, b, se, df, p,
              expected = -1),
  piecewise |>
    transmute(test = str_c("piecewise, ", training, " training"), outcome,
              b, se, df, p,
              expected = if_else(training == "experimental", 1, -1))
) |>
  mutate(p_one_sided = pt(expected * b / se, df, lower.tail = FALSE))

Does the result hold if the p-values are corrected for testing many outcomes? The Benjamini-Hochberg correction within each test, over the 23 scales and, as a family of their own, over the three composites (one per hypothesis); for the two-sided and for the one-sided p:

directional <- directional |>
  mutate(family = if_else(outcome %in% scales$scale, "scales",
                          "composites")) |>
  mutate(p_BH           = p.adjust(p, method = "BH"),
         p_one_sided_BH = p.adjust(p_one_sided, method = "BH"),
         .by = c(test, family))

The confirmatory test, the interaction at T1, with its four p-values:

directional |>
  filter(test == "preregistered, T1") |>
  select(outcome, b, p, p_one_sided, p_BH, p_one_sided_BH) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))

How many effects in the expected direction are significant? Per test, two-sided and one-sided, without and with the correction:

directional_count <- directional |>
  mutate(towards = expected * b > 0) |>    # in the expected direction
  summarise(two_sided    = sum(p < .05 & towards),
            one_sided    = sum(p_one_sided < .05),
            two_sided_BH = sum(p_BH < .05 & towards),
            one_sided_BH = sum(p_one_sided_BH < .05),
            .by = c(family, test))

One-sided, 12 instead of 10 scales reach significance at T1 (Belongingness and Intellectual Capital join, both p = .035 one-sided), and so do all three composites: besides Cognitive Complexity, also Listening and Togetherness and Well-being (p = .030 and .042). No Alienation, significant against the training, counts in no column. The correction costs more than the one-sided test gains: of the 10 two-sided effects at T1, 7 remain (8 one-sided), of the 5 at T2 none (2 one-sided). In the replication window, the period-specific model keeps 6 of its 8 scale effects and the piecewise model 8 of 8. Among the three hypotheses, Cognitive Complexity at T1 holds under every variant; Listening and Togetherness and Well-being at T1 hold only one-sided, there also after the correction.

10.8 All outcomes at a glance

How do the training effects compare? One row per outcome: the interaction at each wave (step 3), the period-specific term with its singular fits and the two piecewise terms (step 5), each as b (p):

glance_period <- period_specific |>
  transmute(outcome, period_T3 = b_and_p(b, p), singular)

glance_piecewise <- piecewise |>
  transmute(outcome, training = str_c("piecewise_", training),
            effect = b_and_p(b, p)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = training, values_from = effect)

interactions |>
  transmute(outcome, wave, effect = b_and_p(b, p)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = wave, values_from = effect) |>
  left_join(glance_period, by = "outcome") |>
  left_join(glance_piecewise, by = "outcome") |>
  mutate(outcome = label_of(outcome))

And the random structure and the claims of absence? First the null models, the trainer level and the equivalence tests of the 26 sections, each brought together in one table:

random_structure <- tibble(
  outcome    = outcomes,
  AIC_nested = unname(map_dbl(from_sections("null_nested"), AIC)),
  AIC_person = unname(map_dbl(from_sections("null_person"), AIC))) |>
  mutate(better = if_else(AIC_nested <= AIC_person, "Municipality/id",
                          "id"))

trainer_shares <- from_sections("trainer_shares") |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "outcome") |>
  filter(level == "trainedBy") |>
  select(outcome, trainer_share = share)

trainer_comparison <- tibble(
  outcome          = outcomes,
  AIC_municipality = unname(map_dbl(from_sections("model"), AIC)),
  AIC_trainer      = unname(map_dbl(from_sections("trainer"), AIC))) |>
  left_join(trainer_shares, by = "outcome")

both_structures <- from_sections("interactions") |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "outcome") |>
  transmute(outcome, wave = str_extract(term, "T[1-3]"), b, p, b_trainer,
            p_trainer)

# both structures of step 7; per outcome first the claim after both
# trainings, then the one at baseline
tost <- from_sections("tost") |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "outcome") |>
  arrange(match(outcome, outcomes), claim)

equivalence <- tost |>
  filter(model == "preregistered") |>
  select(outcome, claim, term, delta_d, se_d, ci_low, ci_high, p_tost,
         p_two_sided, verdict)

richest_structures <- tibble(
  outcome   = outcomes,
  structure = as.character(from_sections("richest")))

equivalence_richest <- tost |>
  filter(model == "richest") |>
  left_join(richest_structures, by = "outcome") |>
  select(outcome, structure, claim, term, delta_d, se_d, ci_low, ci_high,
         p_tost, p_two_sided, verdict)

Then one row per outcome: the level AIC prefers in the null models, the share of the variance between municipalities, how much the trainer level changes the AIC and how much of the variance it takes up (step 2), the richest structure, and Δd with its 90 % interval for both claims of absence (step 7):

glance_shares <- from_sections("shares") |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "outcome") |>
  filter(level == "Municipality") |>
  select(outcome, municipality_share = share)

glance_trainer <- trainer_comparison |>
  transmute(outcome, trainer_AIC = AIC_trainer - AIC_municipality,
            trainer_share)

glance_tost <- equivalence |>
  transmute(outcome, claim,
            interval = d_and_ci(delta_d, ci_low, ci_high)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = claim, values_from = interval)

random_structure |>
  select(outcome, AIC_prefers = better) |>
  left_join(glance_shares, by = "outcome") |>
  left_join(glance_trainer, by = "outcome") |>
  left_join(richest_structures, by = "outcome") |>
  left_join(glance_tost, by = "outcome") |>
  select(outcome, AIC_prefers, municipality_share, trainer_AIC,
         trainer_share, richest = structure, baseline, after_both) |>
  mutate(outcome = label_of(outcome),
         across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))

Is the municipality a level of its own?

AIC prefers persons alone for 4 outcomes (Positivity Resonance, Belongingness, Rogerian Schema, and Relatedness Satisfaction). All models keep the municipality level nevertheless: the conditions were assigned by municipality, so the design calls for it, whatever its share of variance.

Does the trainer level change the results? Per wave, the significant interactions of the 23 scales under both structures, and the largest shift of b:

both_structures |>
  filter(outcome %in% scales$scale) |>
  summarise(significant         = sum(p < .05),
            significant_trainer = sum(p_trainer < .05),
            largest_shift_b     = round(max(abs(b_trainer - b)), 3),
            .by = wave)
wave significant significant_trainer largest_shift_b
T1 11 11 0.005
T2 5 5 0.006
T3 2 2 0.008

AIC prefers the models without the trainer level for 25 of the 26 outcomes; only for Flourishing does the trainer level lower it, by 1.0 points. The trainers carry at most 2.3 % of the variance, for many outcomes none. The interaction terms move by at most 0.008 and no test changes its verdict, so the counts of significant effects hold with either structure; step 7 of each outcome finds the same for the equivalence tests.

What do the interactions show across the outcomes?

At T1, 10 scales show a significant interaction in favour of the experimental group, led by Others Listen to Me, Paradox Mindset, and I Listen (b = 0.82, 0.71, 0.60); No Alienation again moves against the training (b = -0.76). By T2, 5 interactions remain significant: the advantage fades before the control group trains. At T3, 2 interactions are significantly negative, as the freshly trained control group catches up. Of the composites, only Cognitive Complexity (H2) shows a significant interaction at T1 (b = 0.31).

Does the effect replicate when the control group trains?

The piecewise model shows the crossover of the wait-list design: 9 scales rise significantly in the experimental group’s training window, 8 fall in the control group’s window (the control group gains more), and the composites Listening and Togetherness and Cognitive Complexity are significant in both.

Does the change vary between trainers, municipalities and persons? The random slopes of the composites across trainers and municipalities (step 6):

slopes <- tibble(outcome = composites,
                 test    = list(h1_slope_test, h2_slope_test,
                                h3_slope_test)) |>
  mutate(test = map(test, \(t) t[2, ])) |>
  unnest(test) |>
  select(outcome, chisq = Chisq, df = Df, p = `Pr(>Chisq)`)

slopes |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))
outcome chisq df p
H1_ListeningTogetherness 9.467 10 0.488
H2_CognitiveComplexity 16.884 10 0.077
H3_Wellbeing 4.735 10 0.908

None of the three composites shows significant slope variance across trainers and municipalities. Condition varies between municipalities and is not in these models, so slope variance at the municipality level would partly express the training effect itself rather than differences between trainers. Within each condition, the 208 tests of all outcomes:

slopes_within |>
  summarise(tests = n(), significant = sum(p < .05),
            smallest_p = round(min(p), 3), .by = c(test, condition))
test condition tests significant smallest_p
slopes, municipalities Experimental 26 2 0.019
slope T0 vs. later, persons Experimental 26 8 0.000
slope T3 vs. earlier, persons Experimental 26 2 0.008
municipality x pre/post Experimental 26 0 0.058
slopes, municipalities Control 26 2 0.001
slope T0 vs. later, persons Control 26 9 0.000
slope T3 vs. earlier, persons Control 26 13 0.000
municipality x pre/post Control 26 0 0.146

Between municipalities the change hardly varies within a condition: 4 of the 52 slope tests are significant, about as many as chance alone gives at α = .05 (2.6), and in no outcome do the ten municipalities of an arm gain differently from their training (smallest p = .058). Between persons the change does vary: 32 of the 104 person-level tests are significant, 21 of the 52 for the contrast of the arm’s own training (T0 against later in the experimental group, T3 against earlier in the control group). The training thus works about alike in the ten municipalities of each condition, while persons differ in how much they change. A person-level slope also takes up differences in the spread of the answers between waves, so it marks individual differences in change only roughly.

Can any claim of absence be shown? The verdicts of the 52 equivalence tests (step 7):

equivalence |>
  count(claim, verdict) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = claim, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)
verdict after_both baseline
different 2 2
inconclusive 24 24

No claim of absence can be shown as equivalence: the 90 % intervals are about 0.43 units of Δd wide, wider than the band of ±0.20 itself. Most tests are inconclusive; the groups differ for Kama Muta and Intellectual Humility after both trainings and for Others Listen to Me and Competence Satisfaction at baseline. The intervals, not the verdicts, are the result to report.

Does the verdict depend on the random structure? How often the rule of step 7 keeps each structure, and the verdicts with the richest one:

richest_structures |>
  count(structure)
structure n
(1 | Municipality/id) 15
(1 | id) 1
(1 | trainedBy/Municipality/id) 10 
equivalence_richest |>
  count(claim, verdict) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = claim, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)
verdict after_both baseline
different 2 2
inconclusive 24 24

The rule keeps the trainer level for 10 outcomes, the municipality level for 15 and persons alone for 1. No verdict changes: every test lands where it did with the preregistered structure, the four differences included, and Δd moves by at most 0.005.

Chapter 11 estimates the training effects once more, on the latent means of each construct, with the measurement held equal over the waves and the groups.

saveRDS(list(interactions = interactions, piecewise = piecewise,
             period_specific = period_specific, slopes = slopes,
             equivalence = equivalence,
             trainer_comparison = trainer_comparison,
             both_structures = both_structures,
             slopes_within = slopes_within,
             equivalence_richest = equivalence_richest,
             directional = directional),
        "cache/multilevel.rds")

Read me What this report documents and what each chapter holds.

Part A — Data

From Questionnaires to the Analysis File 79 Excel files, code corrections, double entries, and the case log. Scales and Analysis Datasets Reverse coding, scale composites, long and wide data. Sample Participants, waves, municipalities, and sample sets. Data Quality Careless responding, two flags, and the search for double entries.

Part B — Measurement

Reliability and Baseline Correlations Reliability per wave and correlations at baseline. Measurement Models per Wave Confirmatory factor models at each wave (T0–T3). Measurement Invariance over Time Configural, metric, and scalar invariance across the waves. Simultaneous Block Models Block CFAs: discriminant validity and block-level invariance.

Part C — Training Effects (Preregistered)

Means and Δd Means by condition and wave, and standardized change. Multilevel Models Treatment effects, replication, and sensitivity. Latent Difference-in-Differences Latent DiD in structured means models. Serial Mediation Serial mediation chain: H1 → H2 → H3. Movers Classification of individual change. Robustness across Sample Sets The training effects on the sample sets S0 to S9.

Part D — Post Hoc

Item Pruning Reduction and cleanup of the item pool. Exploratory Graph Analysis Dimensional structure via network psychometrics. Redundancy & IRT Redundancy analysis (UVA) and graded response models. Final Structure The final item pool, its communities, factors and composites. Training Effects on the New Structure Δd, multilevel models and mediation on the two factors. Synthesis Integration of all findings.

Part E — Appendix

Item-Level Δd The training effects item by item, ranked. Software Versions R, Quarto and every package with its version. Requests and Their Status What the team asked for, in plain words, and where it stands.
